Thorough ablation studies (Tables IV-V) demonstrating the contribution of each component and their synergy

Critical acknowledged limitation: performance constrained by feature-based correspondence extraction quality; no robust evaluation of behavior with poor initial correspondences or minimal inlier ratios

strengths: Well-motivated dual-space paradigm effectively combines feature-based and geometry-based correspondence strengths, with clear articulation of complementary advantages

Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets (3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, KITTI) with comparison to 11 state-of-the-art methods and strong empirical results, particularly on accuracy metrics (RMSE, RE, TE)
Significant practical efficiency improvements with 32× speedup over MAC while maintaining comparable or better accuracy through clever 1-point RANSAC reducing O(n³) to O(n) sampling
Thorough technical contributions including symmetry disambiguation, robust point-to-plane filtering, and adaptive Gaussian weighting for outlier handling

Excellent presentation with clear methodology, effective visualizations showing inlier ratio progression, extensive ablation studies (Tables 2-3), and detailed parameter sensitivity analysis demonstrating robustness
Strong versatility demonstrated through compatibility with both hand-crafted (FPFH) and learned (FCGF) features across multiple datasets
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: 1-point RANSAC is directly from prior work (TCF), with claimed differentiation through only incremental modifications (consensus set definition, subset selection criteria, symmetry checking) rather than fundamental innovations

Insufficient theoretical justification for critical design choices: Equation (10) lacks principled motivation, 40% threshold for C̄_II appears arbitrary, Gaussian weighting (Eq. 11) borrowed without ablation, and dual-space formulation lacks clear optimality argument

Dataset-specific parameter tuning contradicts robustness claims: parameter α requires significantly different values (0.2 for 3DMatch vs. 0.95 for 3DLoMatch), λ balances as 0.05 vs. 1.0, limiting true dataset-agnostic applicability despite sensitivity analysis
Strong dependency on initial correspondence quality with acknowledged limitation on extremely low inlier ratios; no systematic analysis of robustness degradation as initial inlier ratio decreases
Marginal improvements in registration recall on challenging scenarios: 41.66% vs. MAC++'s 44.58% on 3DLoMatch (FPFH), reflecting trade-off between accuracy and recall that merits deeper discussion

Incomplete analysis of method characteristics: missing failure case analysis, insufficient discussion of scene types where method struggles, limited runtime bottleneck identification, and no systematic evaluation of normal estimation sensitivity across varying point cloud densities

Generalization limitations: only evaluated on 3D rigid registration; applicability to other domains or modalities unexplored, and parameters appear specifically tuned to 3D point cloud characteristics

Design justifications lack rigor: why construct proxies as anchor neighborhoods versus other geometric structures, unclear convergence behavior of alternating correspondence-weight updates, arbitrary termination criteria (ε=0.001, K_III=200)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with extensive comparisons (10+ methods) and thorough ablation studies that clearly demonstrate component contributions

Well-motivated problem combining feature-based and geometry-based correspondence strengths with computational efficiency gains demonstrated (e.g., 16x speedup over MAC on 3DLoMatch while maintaining competitive accuracy)

Technical implementation quality with C++ implementation, detailed parameter sensitivity analysis (Appendix B.5), and robustness testing across different normal estimation methods and inlier ratio ranges
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of the method pipeline and systematic ablation studies showing marginal but consistent contributions from each component
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The 1-point RANSAC filtering builds directly on TCF [38], differing only in minor details (consensus set definition, subset selection, symmetry checking). The dual-space combination (Eq. 10) is simply a weighted sum with no theoretical justification for this formulation or analysis of optimality

Marginal and inconsistent empirical improvements: On 3DLoMatch (the more challenging benchmark), the method underperforms MAC++ (41.66% vs 44.58% recall with FPFH), contradicting claims of state-of-the-art performance. Improvements are often <1% and dataset-specific

Fundamental unresolved limitations: The acknowledged failure on extremely low-inlier-ratio scenarios (where 'inlier set must be larger than any outlier cluster') is a critical constraint of RANSAC-based methods that is identified but not addressed

Inconsistent experimental claims and setup issues: Abstract claims '32x CPU-time speedup over MAC' but Table 1 shows only ~4x for FCGF on 3DMatch; TurboReg speedup is estimated indirectly rather than measured; learning-based GPU methods included in comparisons despite different computing platforms

Lack of principled design: Parameter λ requires dramatic dataset-dependent tuning (0.05 for indoor, 1.0 for outdoor), and α values vary significantly (0.2, 0.9, 0.95 across datasets), suggesting the weighting strategy lacks theoretical foundation and requires manual tuning

Incomplete technical justification: No computational complexity analysis, no theoretical analysis of why the specific dual-space formulation is optimal, no convergence guarantees for the iterative solver, and missing ablations on alternative objective formulations

Terminology and framing issues: 'Dual-space' misleadingly suggests two geometric spaces when the method operates in a single space; 'Reinforcement' in the title is undefined and never justified; overclaiming on 'state-of-the-art' status when improvements are selective and marginal

strengths: Well-motivated dual-space paradigm clearly addressing complementary limitations of feature-space and geometry-space correspondences
Comprehensive experimental validation across three major benchmarks (3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, KITTI) with both hand-crafted and learned features
State-of-the-art precision metrics: best rotation/translation errors on multiple datasets (e.g., RE=1.75°, TE=6.19cm on 3DMatch FPFH)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3) demonstrating contribution of each component with clear performance degradation when components removed
Extensive robustness analysis including sensitivity to 5 key parameters, varying inlier ratios, and normal estimation variations, showing stable performance across ranges
Thoughtful engineering details including symmetry disambiguation in 1-point RANSAC and probability-weighted refinement
Strong practical efficiency with 32× speedup over MAC and competitive runtimes vs. fastest baselines
High reproducibility: detailed implementation descriptions, algorithm pseudocode, parameter documentation, and supplementary material
Effective speed-accuracy tradeoff balancing precision and computational cost across diverse scenarios
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty—core components (1-point RANSAC, probability-weighted 3-point RANSAC, dual-space weighted optimization) are refinements of prior work (TCF [38], BANSAC [30]) rather than novel methodologies

Actual speedup vs. fastest baseline (TCF) is modest (1.75-1.83× on 3DMatch/3DLoMatch) despite emphasis on efficiency; 32× speedup over MAC is misleading since MAC is inherently slow due to NP-hard clique finding
Registration recall noticeably lower than MAC++ on 3DLoMatch (41.66% vs. 44.58%), suggesting limitations in challenging low-overlap scenarios despite strong precision metrics

Dataset-specific parameter tuning required for optimal performance (α: 0.2→0.95 across datasets, λ: 0.05→1.0), indicating the method is specialized rather than general-purpose despite robustness analysis
Insufficient failure mode analysis—acknowledges struggles with extremely low inlier ratios but lacks empirical characterization of edge cases and failure scenarios
Geometric proxy construction (radius β=50× resolution) chosen empirically without principled theoretical justification; limited comparison with alternative proxy construction methods
No statistical rigor—results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; appears to be single runs rather than multiple trials with variance reporting
Weak comparison with learning-based methods (PointDSC, VBReg) due to GPU time exclusion; may underestimate competitive position of learning approaches on modern hardware
Termination criterion (Eq. 6) depends on estimated inlier ratio which may be unreliable early in iterations; no convergence analysis provided
